rejected.title: Measuring the labour market
card: Unemployment rate
the unemployed as a share of the labour force. The unemployed have no job and are actively looking and available for work. The labour force is everyone aged 15 and over who is employed or unemployed.
Participation rate
the labour force as a share of the civilian population aged 15 and over. It shows how many people are working or seeking work.
Under-utilisation rate
the unemployed plus the underemployed, as a share of the labour force. Underemployed people have a job but want more hours.
The bases differ. The unemployment and under-utilisation rates divide by the labour force. The participation rate divides by the population aged 15 and over.
rejected.remember: The unemployment rate counts jobless people actively looking for work. Under-utilisation also adds people who want more hours.

a.q: Ana's hours are cut from full-time to 10 hours a week, and she wants more work. Which measure rises?
a.why: Ana still has a job, so she is not unemployed and stays in the labour force. She is now underemployed, which the under-utilisation rate adds in. The unemployment rate does not change, because she is still employed.
a.clue: Does Ana still have a job?

b.q: A region's labour force is 200,000. Of these, 10,000 are unemployed and 14,000 are underemployed. What are the two rates?
b.why: Unemployment is 10,000 ÷ 200,000 = 5%. Under-utilisation adds the two groups: 24,000 ÷ 200,000 = 12%. The 7% option uses only the underemployed, but under-utilisation counts the unemployed too.

draft.title: Measuring the labour market
card: Unemployment rate
the unemployed as a share of the labour force. The labour force is everyone aged 15 and over who is employed or actively looking for work.
Participation rate
the labour force as a share of the civilian population aged 15 and over. It shows how many people are working or seeking work.
Under-utilisation rate
the unemployed plus the underemployed, as a share of the labour force. Underemployed people have a job but want more hours.
A person who wants work but has stopped looking is not in the labour force. They leave the unemployment rate, so it can understate the lack of jobs.
draft.remember: Unemployment rate counts the jobless. Under-utilisation also counts people wanting more hours.

a.q: Which measure counts people who have a job but want more hours?
a.why: The under-utilisation rate adds the underemployed to the unemployed. The unemployment rate counts only people with no job who are looking for work, so it leaves out the underemployed.
a.clue: Which measure adds the underemployed to the unemployed?

b.q: In a town, many jobseekers give up looking and leave the labour force, while no one gains or loses a job. What happens to the measured rates?
opts: Unemployment and participation rates both fall
Unemployment rate falls and participation rate rises
Unemployment rate rises and participation rate falls
Unemployment and participation rates both rise
b.why: Discouraged people are no longer in the labour force, so the labour force shrinks. This lowers the participation rate, and the unemployed count falls, so the unemployment rate falls even though no new jobs exist.
b.clue: Someone who stops looking is no longer counted in the labour force.

b.best: Unemployment and participation rates both fall

problems.detail: The last bullet explains hidden (discouraged) unemployment, people who want work but have stopped looking. That term belongs to point 4 (The labour force) and is explained here rather than only mentioned.

Question b rests on hidden unemployment, which is point 4's idea, and its why names 'discouraged' people. It tests another point's concept, although the effect on the measured rates is a fair measurement question.

'Unemployment rate counts the jobless' is looser than the card. The card says jobless people who have stopped looking are not counted, so the line implies all jobless people are included. Better: 'counts jobless people actively looking for work'.

'Counts people who have a job but want more hours' is slightly loose. The participation rate and employment rate also include underemployed people among those they count, just not separately. Wording such as 'adds in' or 'specifically counts' would be tighter.

check.summary: Both answers are correct: under-utilisation for a, and both rates fall for b. The card and question b explain hidden unemployment, which belongs to point 4, and the remember line glosses over the fact that only active jobseekers count as unemployed.

card: Unemployment rate
the number of unemployed people as a share of the labour force. It is the most quoted measure of how many people want work and cannot find it.
Participation rate
the labour force as a share of the civilian population aged 15 and over. It shows how many people are working or seeking work.

the unemployed plus the underemployed, as a share of the labour force. It is wider than the unemployment rate because it adds the underemployed.

draft.remember: The unemployment rate counts only the unemployed. Under-utilisation adds the underemployed to them.

a.q: A region has 10,000 unemployed and 14,000 underemployed people in a labour force of 200,000. What are its two rates?
a.why: Unemployment is 10,000 ÷ 200,000 = 5%. Under-utilisation adds the two groups: 24,000 ÷ 200,000 = 12%. The 7% option uses only the underemployed, but under-utilisation counts the unemployed too.

b.q: A town has a civilian population aged 15 and over of 50,000 and a labour force of 32,000. What is its participation rate?
opts: 64%, found by dividing by the population aged 15 and over
64%, found by dividing by the labour force
36%, found by dividing by the population aged 15 and over
36%, found by dividing by the labour force
b.why: Participation = 32,000 ÷ 50,000 = 64%. The base is the population aged 15 and over, not the labour force. The labour force is the part being counted, so dividing by it would not make sense.
b.clue: Which group is the base for the participation rate?

b.best: 64%, found by dividing by the population aged 15 and over
